title: Scams: fake prizes, loans and job offers
essentialQuestion: How can you tell when a message is trying to trick people?
learningGoal: Identify the warning signs of a scam in made-up messages, and explain what to do instead of replying.

warmUp.question: A message says someone won a prize, but they never entered a competition. What do you think?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Which messages ask for money or private information? Which one does not?

sections.heading: Scams pretend to be good news
sections.text: A scam is a trick to get someone's money or private information. Scam messages can reach anyone, including people you know, so it helps everyone when you can spot them. Many scams pretend to bring good news, such as a prize, an easy loan or a job that pays very well. Scammers sometimes pretend to be from an organisation that people know and trust. In Stonebridge, Message A says that someone has won a new tablet. But nobody entered a competition. A prize that you never tried to win is the first warning sign.
sections.simpler: A scam is a trick. It tries to get money or private information. Scam messages can come to anyone. Many scams look like good news. They offer a prize, an easy loan or a great job. Some scammers pretend to be a group you trust. In Stonebridge, Message A says someone won a new tablet. But nobody tried to win one. That is the first warning sign.

sections.heading: Look for warning signs
sections.text: Most scam messages share a few warning signs. First, they ask you to pay before you get anything. Real prizes are free, and honest employers do not ask people to pay for work. Second, they push you to hurry, with words like “today only” or “ends in one hour”, so you don't stop to think. Third, they sound too good to be true, like lots of money for very little work. Fourth, they ask for private information, such as a home address or everything on a phone. Message B offers easy loans to everyone and wants to see all the contacts and photos on a phone. Illegal lenders often ask for this.
sections.simpler: Scam messages often have warning signs. One: they ask you to pay first. Real prizes are free. Honest jobs do not cost money to get. Two: they tell you to hurry. Then you don't stop and think. Three: they sound too good to be true. Four: they ask for private information. Message B offers easy loans to everyone. It wants to see all the photos on a phone. Illegal lenders often ask for this.

sections.heading: What to do instead
sections.text: If a message shows warning signs, don't reply, don't pay and don't send any information. Instead, talk to someone you trust, such as a teacher, and show them the message. If a message says it comes from an organisation you know, contact that organisation in a way you already know, not through the message. Then you can warn other people, so they don't get tricked too. Message D, from the notice board at the Stonebridge Learning Centre, shows no warning signs. The art club is free, nobody needs to hurry, and you can ask Ms Ada in person. If you are not sure, it is always fine to ask.
sections.simpler: See warning signs? Don't reply. Don't pay. Don't send information. Show the message to someone you trust, like a teacher. Does it say it comes from a group you know? Then contact that group yourself. Don't use the message. Then warn other people. Message D has no warning signs. The art club is free. Nobody has to hurry. You can ask Ms Ada in person.

glossary.definition: A trick to get people's money or private information.
glossary.example: Message A, the prize message, is a scam.

glossary.definition: Facts about a person that can show exactly who or where they are.
glossary.example: A full name and a home address are private information.

glossary.definition: Money you borrow and must pay back later.
glossary.example: Message B offers easy loans to everyone.

glossary.definition: Something that tells you there may be danger or a trick.
glossary.example: “Pay a joining fee to start” is a warning sign.
Illegal lenders often ask to see everything on a phone.

checks.question: What is the biggest warning sign in Message A?

options.text: It was sent in the morning
options.feedback: Not quite. The time is not a warning sign. Look at what the message asks you to do.

options.text: It is about a new tablet
options.feedback: Not quite. A tablet is not the problem. Look at what you must do to get it.

options.text: You must pay for a prize
options.feedback: Yes. Real prizes are free. If you must pay to get a prize, it is a scam.

checks.question: You think a message might be a scam. What is a good next step?

options.text: Reply and ask if it is real
options.feedback: Not quite. Don't reply to the message. Read the third section about what to do instead.
Yes. Showing the message to a teacher or another person you trust is a safe next step.

options.text: Pay a little to find out
options.feedback: Not quite. Never pay to check. Read the third section about what to do instead.

watch.title: Is this a scam? Investment episode
watch.why: It is a short cartoon quiz show from a government office. It shows a message that is too good to be true.
watch.beforeQuestion: What would make you think a message is too good to be true?
watch.afterQuestion: What did the host say to do with the email?
watch.summary: This short cartoon looks like a quiz show on television. The host shows an email from a company. It offers a way to make money that is “risk-free”, with “guaranteed” returns in one month. It also asks to invest money for you. The host asks what you should do. Should you send your money? Should you write back and ask for more information? Or should you delete the email and warn your friends? You have three seconds to decide. The answer is to delete the email and warn other people. The host says the email was too good to be true. She says never let anyone pressure you into a decision about money. Always get advice from someone who is not part of the offer.
keyPoints: An offer that sounds too good to be true is a warning sign.
Don't let anyone push you into a quick decision about money.
Delete the message and warn other people.
watch.contentNote: A cartoon quiz show from Consumer Affairs Victoria, a government office in Australia. It is about an investment email, which learners may not have met, but the warning signs are the same as in the lesson. The summary was checked against the office's own written transcript; the length is not confirmed. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Learners may know someone who lost money or was tricked. Don't ask about it. If a learner describes a real message or loss, don't debate the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process. Being tricked is never something to be ashamed of.

Fake job offers are linked to serious exploitation: a UN human rights report (2023) found that hundreds of thousands of people in Southeast Asia had been trafficked into scam operations, many through false job offers. The lesson keeps the job example to a simple “pay to start” message on purpose. Never use examples about work in another place, papers, resettlement, visas, legal status, aid or official services. A partner educator must review this lesson before use.
educatorNotes: For reviewers (spec section 8, item 5): learners aged 10–17 may not be allowed to work or borrow, so the loan and job messages are framed as messages anyone might get. Swap them if the partner prefers. In Indonesia, OJK warns that illegal online lenders send messages people didn't ask for and ask to see far more of a phone than they need (Antara, 2021); a partner could localise Message B.
All four messages are made up and can't work as real scams: no links, numbers, bank names or payment details. Paper version of the activity: print the messages and underline the warning signs.
